        .add_event(AxelarnetGatewayEvent::MessageExecuted { msg }.into()))

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The BaseAmplifierGateway contract does not implement role-based access control (RBAC) on its critical functions related to message approval, validation, and execution. 

This vulnerability allows anyone (including malicious attackers) to interact directly with these functions and potentially issue harmful or compromising the contract's integrity.

In this contract, the `callContract`, `validateMessage`, and `_approveMessage` functions are all unprotected, permitting any address to execute these actions without control.

For example the function `_approveMessage(Message calldata message)` allows the updating of the state variable `messages` from the `BaseAmplifierGatewayStorage` struct. 

This function does not have any access control mechanisms such as `onlyOwner` or `onlyAdmin` modifiers, thus it can be called by any account on the network, increasing the risk of malicious and unintended changes to the contract's state.

## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/main/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/BaseAmplifierGateway.sol#L146-L154

```solidity
function _approveMessage(Message calldata message) internal {
    bytes32 commandId = messageToCommandId(message.sourceChain, message.messageId);
    if (_baseAmplifierGatewayStorage().messages[commandId] != MESSAGE_NONEXISTENT) { return; }
    bytes32 messageHash = _messageHash( commandId, message.sourceChain, message.sourceAddress, message.contractAddress, message.payloadHash );
     _baseAmplifierGatewayStorage().messages[commandId] = messageHash; 
     emit MessageApproved( commandId, message.sourceChain, message.messageId, message.sourceAddress, message.contractAddress, message.payloadHash ); 
}


## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Role-based access control should be implemented to dictate permissions for every external and internal function within the contract. 

Consider using OpenZeppelin's `AccessControl` library for this purpose, which allows for easy management of roles and permissions. A set of well-defined roles should be created, and these roles should be checked before executing critical functions. 


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `_validateSignatures` function might be subject to a Denial of Service (DoS) attack by the Block Gas Limit. 

As this function requires both signers and signatures to be sorted for operation, a large number of signers and signatures could make the `for-loop` excessively gas-consuming, resulting in exceeding the block gas limit, making it impractical or impossible in some cases.

## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/main/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/governance/BaseWeightedMultisig.sol#L192-L234

The function `_validateSignatures` has a nested `for-loop`:

```solidity
    for (uint256 i; i < signaturesLength; ++i) {
        address recoveredSigner = ECDSA.recover(messageHash, signatures[i]);

        // looping through remaining signers to find a match
        for (; signerIndex < signersLength && recoveredSigner != signers[signerIndex].signer; ++signerIndex) {}

        // checking if we are out of signers
        if (signerIndex == signersLength) revert MalformedSignatures();
       ...
```

This function iterates through each signature, recovers the signer from the signature, and then iterates through the list of signers to find a match. 

If the list of signatures and signers is too large, this loop could exceed Ethereum's block gas limit, causing the transaction to fail due to the computational heaviness of ECDSA.recover().


## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

For instance, an option could be to use a mapping to check if a signer is in the signers list. But this would require maintaining the signers list and the mapping in sync. As there is no inherent ordering in a mapping, some changes would need to take place to ensure that signers are presented in an ascending manner.

Another way of handling it is by setting a limit on the number of signers and signatures. This limit should be set according to the block gas limit and the amount of gas the rest of the operations in the function need.



## Assessed type

DoS

In the function `deployInterchainToken`, tokens are first minted and then the minter's address is transferred. The function `token.mint` and `token.transferMintership` are external calls that can be a potential target of reentrancy risk.

function deployInterchainToken(

    string calldata symbol,
    uint8 decimals,
    uint256 initialSupply,

    ...

    ...
}

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/main/interchain-token-service/contracts/token-manager/TokenManager.sol#L117
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/main/interchain-token-service/contracts/utils/FlowLimit.sol#L18


# Vulnerability details

**Impact**
Interchain tokens in the protocol have a `flowLimit` minimising the amount of tokens that can be added/removed from a particular chain over a set period of time (referred to as an `EPOCH`, each of which is 6 hours long). This is however exploitable as a user with enough tokens could transfer the maximum repeatedly causing interchain transfers to a particular chain to be DoSed.

This behaviour is damaging regardless, however one way it could be particularly harmful to users is when considering a user triggering an `expressExecute` of an interchain transfer. When performing an `expressExecute` the caller on the destination chain will first transfer their own tokens (ones already on the chain) to the recipient with the expectation that they will be reimbursed shortly afterwards once the transaction has been finalised on the source chain. However in the DoS scenario outlined above this denial of service would delay the express executor getting their tokens reimbursed. This is particularly problematic when considering the differences in block finality wait periods across chain as shown in the Axelar docs [here](https://github.com/axelarnetwork/axelar-docs/blob/main/src/pages/learn/txduration.mdx), as attackers can use chains with fast block finality to DoS interchain transfers from chains with slower block finality.

**Proof Of Concept**
Consider the following steps:
1. User A triggers an interchain token transfer moving tokens from Chain A to Chain B (where Chain A is a chain with slower block finality).
2. User B (potentially a protocol willing to put up the tokens) triggers the `InterchainTokenService::expressExecute` transferring the tokens to the recipient on the destination chain.

## Vulnerability Details
InterchainMultisig inherits from BaseWeightedMultisig. This means it inherits all the state variables and functions, including the storage layout defined in the base contract. InterchainMultisig introduces its own storage struct, InterchainMultisigStorage, and uses a similar pattern to calculate its dedicated storage slot (INTERCHAIN_MULTISIG_SLOT).

Here's how both BaseWeightedMultisig and InterchainMultisig calculate their storage slots.
- BaseWeightedMultisig uses keccak256('BaseWeightedMultisig.Slot') - 1.
- InterchainMultisig uses keccak256('InterchainMultisig.Slot') - 1.

This approach only works well as long as the contract is not inherited and extended by other contracts that also employ a similar storage slot calculation mechanism.

There's a possibility, although slim, that these hash calculations might result in the same value. If that happens, both BaseWeightedMultisigStorage and InterchainMultisigStorage would attempt to occupy the same storage slot, leading to a collision.

Hash functions like keccak256 take an input and produce a fixed-size output (a hash). Ideally, different inputs should produce different hashes. A collision occurs when two different inputs produce the same hash output. While hash functions are designed to minimize collisions, they are not entirely impossible. The probability of a collision increases more rapidly than one might intuitively expect. This is related to the Birthday Paradox, which states that in a group of just 23 people, there's a greater than 50% chance that two people share the same birthday.


## Code
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/governance/BaseWeightedMultisig.sol#L15

        0x457f3fc26bf430b020fe76358b1bfaba57e1657ace718da6437cda9934eabfe8;

```

## Scenario

The storage slot calculation involves:

- Taking a string literal (e.g., 'BaseWeightedMultisig.Slot' or 'InterchainMultisig.Slot')
- Passing it to keccak256 to get a hash
- Subtracting 1 from the hash result

The potential collision arises because:

- The input strings are different, but they have a similar structure.
- keccak256 produces a 256-bit hash, which has a vast number of possible outputs (2^256).
- However, the final step of subtracting 1 slightly reduces the range of possible outputs.

While the probability of these specific strings resulting in the same hash after the subtraction is low, it's not zero.


## Impact

If a collision does occur:

BASE_WEIGHTED_MULTISIG_SLOT and INTERCHAIN_MULTISIG_SLOT would have the same value.
When the contracts are deployed and their storage is initialized, both BaseWeightedMultisigStorage and InterchainMultisigStorage would try to write their data to the same storage slot.
This would lead to data overwriting and corruption.
The contract's behavior would become unpredictable and likely erroneous, as the state variables it relies on would be incorrect.


## Fix

Ensure that the storage slots for both structs are distinct. Here are a couple of approaches:

1. Incorporate a unique salt or identifier into the hash calculation, preferably something tied to the contract's identity. For example:
    
```Solidity
// In BaseWeightedMultisig
bytes32 internal constant BASE_WEIGHTED_MULTISIG_SLOT = keccak256(abi.encodePacked("BaseWeightedMultisig.Slot", uint256(type(BaseWeightedMultisig).creationCode)));

// In InterchainMultisig
bytes32 internal constant INTERCHAIN_MULTISIG_SLOT = keccak256(abi.encodePacked("InterchainMultisig.Slot", uint256(type(InterchainMultisig).creationCode)));
```

This leverages the type(Contract).creationCode feature, which returns the contract's creation bytecode. This ensures a high degree of uniqueness, as the creation bytecode is specific to each contract, even if they share the same source code.

2. If you anticipate more structs being added in future extensions or upgrades, a hierarchical approach can provide better organization and collision avoidance:


```Solidity
// In BaseWeightedMultisig
bytes32 internal constant BASE_SLOT = keccak256(abi.encodePacked("MyContracts.Base"));
bytes32 internal constant BASE_WEIGHTED_MULTISIG_SLOT = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(BASE_SLOT, "WeightedMultisig"));

// In InterchainMultisig
bytes32 internal constant INTERCHAIN_MULTISIG_SLOT = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(BASE_SLOT, "InterchainMultisig"));
```

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

The `permit` function is designed to allow users to approve token spending without sending a transaction, using a signed message instead. This is part of the ERC20Permit standard (EIP-2612).

The function increments the nonce after using it in the message digest calculation:

```solidity
keccak256(abi.encode(PERMIT_SIGNATURE_HASH, issuer, spender, value, nonces[issuer]++, deadline))
```

This creates a race condition where multiple valid signatures for the same nonce can be created and used.

## Code Snippet

```solidity
bytes32 digest = keccak256(
            abi.encodePacked(
                EIP191_PREFIX_FOR_EIP712_STRUCTURED_DATA,
                DOMAIN_SEPARATOR(),
                keccak256(abi.encode(PERMIT_SIGNATURE_HASH, issuer, spender, value, nonces[issuer]++, deadline))
            )
```

## Impact

This vulnerability allows for potential replay attacks. An attacker could use the same signature multiple times if they can front-run the original transaction. Each use would be considered valid because the nonce is only incremented after the signature verification.

## Scenario

1. Alice signs a permit for Bob to spend 100 tokens.

2. Bob sees this signed permit and submits a transaction to use it.

3. An attacker sees Bob's transaction in the mempool and front-runs it with a higher gas price.

4. The attacker's transaction succeeds, using Alice's permit.

5. Bob's original transaction still succeeds because the nonce check passes.

6. Alice's tokens are spent twice, despite only signing once.

## Fix

The nonce should be read and incremented atomically. Here's the corrected code:

```solidity
uint256 currentNonce = nonces[issuer];
nonces[issuer] = currentNonce + 1;
bytes32 digest = keccak256(
    abi.encodePacked(
        EIP191_PREFIX_FOR_EIP712_STRUCTURED_DATA,
        DOMAIN_SEPARATOR(),
        keccak256(abi.encode(PERMIT_SIGNATURE_HASH, issuer, spender, value, currentNonce, deadline))
    )
);
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-amplifier/contracts/axelarnet-gateway/src/contract.rs#L63-L85


# Vulnerability details

## Description
The Axelarnet Gateway contract is initliazed by calling `instantiate()`:
```rust
#[cfg_attr(not(feature = "library"), entry_point)]
pub fn instantiate(
    deps: DepsMut,
    _env: Env,
    _info: MessageInfo,
    msg: InstantiateMsg,
) -> Result<Response, axelar_wasm_std::error::ContractError> {
    cw2::set_contract_version(deps.storage, CONTRACT_NAME, CONTRACT_VERSION)?;

    let router = deps
        .api
        .addr_validate(&msg.router_address)
        .change_context(Error::InvalidAddress(msg.router_address.clone()))?;

    let config = Config {
        chain_name: msg.chain_name,
        router,
    };

    state::save_config(deps.storage, &config).change_context(Error::InvalidStoreAccess)?;

    Ok(Response::new())
}
```

If we take a look at the [Cosmwasm docs](https://docs.cosmwasm.com/docs/smart-contracts/migration), we can find the following:
```md
CosmWasm made contract migration a first-class experience. 
When instantiating a contract, there is an optional admin field that you can set. 
If it is left empty, the contract is immutable. 
If it is set (to an external account or governance contract), that account can trigger a migration. 
The admin can also change admin or even make the contract fully immutable after some time. 
However, when we wish to migrate from contract A to contract B, contract B needs to be aware somehow of how the state was encoded.
```

In the `instantiate()` function shown above, there is no `admin` field set. This means that this contract is immutable and contrary to the intention of the Sponsor, `migrate()` will not be callable:
```rust
#[cfg_attr(not(feature = "library"), entry_point)]
pub fn migrate(
    deps: DepsMut,
    _env: Env,
    _msg: Empty,
) -> Result<Response, axelar_wasm_std::error::ContractError> {
    cw2::set_contract_version(deps.storage, CONTRACT_NAME, CONTRACT_VERSION)?;

    Ok(Response::default())
}
```

This results in a non-upgradeable contract, even though it should be upgradeable, breaking one of the invariants set in the `README.md`.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Set the admin field.


## Assessed type

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-amplifier/interchain-token-service/src/state.rs#L121-L128


# Vulnerability details

## Description
In `interchain-token-service/src/state.rs`, the following function is meant to remove trusted addresses:
```rust
#[cfg(test)]
pub(crate) fn remove_trusted_address(
    storage: &mut dyn Storage,
    chain: &ChainName,
) -> Result<(), Error> {
    TRUSTED_ITS_ADDRESSES.remove(storage, chain);
    Ok(())
}
```

The problem is, as we can see in the code snippet, is that the `#[cfg(test)]` flag is used.

If we take a look at the [Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch11-03-test-organization.html#the-tests-module-and-cfgtest), we can read the following:
```
The `#[cfg(test)]` annotation on the tests module tells Rust to compile and run the test code only when you run `cargo test`, not when you run `cargo build`. This saves compile time when you only want to build the library and saves space in the resulting compiled artifact because the tests are not included.
```

This means during the `cargo build` run, it will **not** include the `remove_trusted_address()` function.

This means if any of the current trusted addresses go rogue, they won't be able to be removed because the `remove_trusted_address()` function is not included in the release binary.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove  `#[cfg(test)]`:
```diff
- #[cfg(test)]
pub(crate) fn remove_trusted_address(
    storage: &mut dyn Storage,
    chain: &ChainName,
) -> Result<(), Error> {
    TRUSTED_ITS_ADDRESSES.remove(storage, chain);
    Ok(())
}
```

Other

Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

The use of incorrect data types in the bytes.concat function leads to a compilation error, preventing the contract from being compiled and deployed. This error stops the contract from functioning as intended and could cause significant issues if the function is critical for contract logic.

## Proof of Concept
Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.

The following error indicates that an invalid type is being used in the bytes.concat function. The function expects a bytes or fixed bytes type, but a string is being provided instead.
```log

TypeError: Invalid type for argument in the bytes.concat function call. bytes or fixed bytes type is required, but string provided.
   --> /Users/williamsmith/Desktop/Stuff/2024-08-axelar-network/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/BaseAmplifierGateway.sol:105:46:

105 |         return keccak256(bytes(string.concat(sourceChain, '_', messageId)));

    function messageToCommandId(string calldata sourceChain, string calldata messageId) public pure returns (bytes32) {

```sol

        // Axelar doesn't allow `sourceChain` to contain '_', hence this encoding is umambiguous
        return keccak256(bytes(bytes.concat(bytes(sourceChain), '_', bytes(messageId))));

```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

The code attempts to decode the first 4 bytes from a bytes calldata slice into a bytes4 and then convert that bytes4 to a uint32. However, Solidity does not allow direct conversion from a bytes calldata slice to bytes4, which results in a fatal compilation error.

This issue prevents the contract from compiling, leading to deployment failure. This not only stops the smart contract from functioning but also halts any further development and testing. In a production environment, this could delay the release of critical updates or fixes.

## Proof of Concept
Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.

Consider the following code snippet that triggers the error:
```sol
uint32 versionUint = uint32(bytes4(metadata[:4]));
```

This code will result in the following error:
```log
[ERROR]: Solc experienced a fatal error.

TypeError: Explicit type conversion not allowed from "bytes calldata slice" to "bytes4".
    --> /2024-08-axelar-network/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol:1128:37:
     |
1128 |         uint32 versionUint = uint32(bytes4(metadata[:4]));
     |                                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

## Tools Used
Manual review and MythX.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The error can be mitigated by using bitwise operations directly on the metadata slice instead of attempting to convert the slice to bytes4. The corrected code snippet avoids the direct conversion and processes each byte individually to construct the uint32 value.
```sol
// Decode the first 4 bytes from metadata
        bytes4 versionBytes4 = abi.decode(metadata[:4], (bytes4));
        // Convert bytes4 to uint32 using bitwise shift
        uint32 versionUint = uint32(uint32(uint8(versionBytes4[0])) << 24 |
                           uint32(uint8(versionBytes4[1])) << 16 |
                           uint32(uint8(versionBytes4[2])) << 8 |
                           uint32(uint8(versionBytes4[3])));
```

Bitwise Operations: 
The corrected code directly accesses each byte in the metadata array, converts it to uint8, and shifts it into place within a uint32 variable.

Avoiding Direct Conversion: 
By manually constructing the uint32 from individual bytes, the code circumvents Solidity’s restriction on direct type conversion from bytes calldata to bytes4.

## Impact
Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

***Prerequisites:
Update all contracts' pragma versions from ^0.8.0 to ^0.8.4 in order for the contracts to subsequently compile after the overrides are implemented.***

The TokenManagerProxy contract contains a function getImplementationTypeAndTokenAddress that overrides a function declared in the ITokenManagerProxy interface. However, the overriding function is missing the override keyword, which is required in Solidity 0.8.0 and later to explicitly denote that a function overrides another function in a base contract or interface.

This issue is causing compilation errors in this contract.

The TokenManagerProxy contract declares public state variables (implementationType, interchainTokenId, and tokenAddress) that override getter functions declared in the ITokenManagerProxy interface. However, the overriding state variables are missing the override keyword.

Solidity requires the override keyword when a public state variable overrides a getter function defined in an interface. Without this, the code will fail to compile, rendering the contract unusable.

## Proof of Concept
Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.

Affected code
```sol
function getImplementationTypeAndTokenAddress() external view returns (uint256 implementationType_, address tokenAddress_) {
    implementationType_ = implementationType;
    tokenAddress_ = tokenAddress;
}

uint256 public immutable implementationType;
bytes32 public immutable interchainTokenId;
address public immutable tokenAddress;
```

Attempting to compile the contract will result in the following error:
```sol
TypeError: Overriding function is missing "override" specifier.
  --> /contracts/proxies/TokenManagerProxy.sol:61:5:
   |
61 |     function getImplementationTypeAndTokenAddress() external view returns (uint256 implementationType_, address tokenAddress_) {
   |     ^ (Relevant source part starts here and spans across multiple lines).

TypeError: Overriding public state variable is missing "override" specifier.
  --> /contracts/proxies/TokenManagerProxy.sol:21:5:
   |
21 |     uint256 public immutable implementationType;
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

22 |     bytes32 public immutable interchainTokenId;
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

TypeError: Overriding public state variable is missing "override" specifier.

23 |     address public immutable tokenAddress;
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

## Tools Used
Manual review and MythX.

To resolve this issue, add the override keyword to the function declaration and public state variables, indicating that it intentionally overrides a function and variables in the interface.
```sol
function getImplementationTypeAndTokenAddress() external view override returns (uint256 implementationType_, address tokenAddress_) {
    implementationType_ = implementationType;
    tokenAddress_ = tokenAddress;
}

uint256 public immutable override implementationType;
bytes32 public immutable override interchainTokenId;
address public immutable override tokenAddress;
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/c383cc0e51805357bca8741ec5d1568cacbff6cc/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/AxelarAmplifierGateway.sol#L132-L134


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

Lack of Zero Address Check in transferOperatorship Function in the AxelarAmplifierGateway contract

The transferOperatorship function allows the current operator or owner to transfer the operator role to a new address. 

However, the transferOperatorship function does not verify if the newOperator is not a zero address (address(0)). 

Assigning the zero address to the operator role can result in the loss of control over the operator-specific functions, potentially leading to governance issues or other critical operational failures.

## Proof of Concept
Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.

Potential loss of contract control due to setting an essential role to a zero address.

Vulnerable Code:
```sol
    function transferOperatorship(address newOperator) external onlyOperatorOrOwner {
        _transferOperatorship(newOperator);
    }
```

Here’s a simplified scenario demonstrating the issue:

1. The current operator calls transferOperatorship with the zero address by mistake or maliciously:
```sol
contract.transferOperatorship(address(0));
```

2. The _transferOperatorship function sets the operator to address(0).

3. Any subsequent actions requiring the operator’s authority would become unexecutable, as address(0) cannot perform transactions or execute functions.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/69c4f2c3fcefb1b8eb2129af9c3685a44ae5b6fe/interchain-token-service/contracts/interchain-token/InterchainToken.sol#L135-L141


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

***Prerequisites:***
1. For all contracts change pragma version from ^0.8.0 to ^0.8.4 in order for contract to compile successfully and subsequently run successfully after overrides keywords are added where necessary.
2. Add override keyword to the functions in contracts that are also in the parents or interfaces.

Allowance Under-run in _spendAllowance Function within InterchainToken contract

The _spendAllowance function in the InterchainToken contract contains a potential arithmetic error that can lead to incorrect allowance handling. 

Specifically, the function subtracts the amount from _allowance without ensuring that amount is less than or equal to _allowance. 

This can result in a subtraction under-run, where the calculated allowance wraps around to a large integer, effectively bypassing the allowance check and allowing the spender to transfer more tokens than intended.

This vulnerability could allow malicious users to spend more tokens than permitted by their allowance, leading to unauthorised token transfers and potential financial loss for token holders.

## Proof of Concept
Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.

***Here is an example illustrating the potential exploit:***

	1.	Assume a spender is granted an allowance of 100 tokens.
	2.	The spender attempts to transfer 150 tokens.
	3.	In the current implementation, this will result in an under-run because _allowance - amount (100 - 150) wraps around to a large number.
	4.	The allowance check is effectively bypassed, allowing the unauthorised transfer of 150 tokens.

***Code Location:***
The vulnerability is located in the _spendAllowance function of the InterchainToken contract:
```sol
    function _spendAllowance(address sender, address spender, uint256 amount) internal override {
        uint256 _allowance = allowance[sender][spender];


        if (_allowance != UINT256_MAX) {
            _approve(sender, spender, _allowance - amount);
        }
    }
```

***Use Case***
The Eminence protocol, created by Andre Cronje, the founder of Yearn Finance, was exploited due to an issue related to the handling of allowances in the smart contract code. 

```URL
https://www.immunebytes.com/blog/eminence-defi-exploit-sep-29-2020-detailed-analysis/

https://sampriestley.com/defi-arbs-explained-15m-eminence-attack/

https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2020/10/01/defi-degens-hit-hard-by-eminence-exploit-will-be-partially-compensated/
```

The hacker exploited a vulnerability in the Eminence contract that allowed them to mint an unlimited amount of EMN tokens. 

This was possible due to a lack of proper validation in the minting process, which is somewhat analogous to the under-run vulnerability where checks on allowances are insufficient or non-existent, allowing unauthorised token transfers.

The result was the draining of $15 million worth of funds from users who had interacted with the smart contract.

## Tools Used
Manual review. 

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this issue, a check should be added to ensure that amount is less than or equal to _allowance before performing the subtraction. 

This can prevent the under-run and ensure that the allowance logic is correctly enforced.

***Mitigation Code***

Here is the revised code for the _spendAllowance function with the necessary check:
```sol
function _spendAllowance(address sender, address spender, uint256 amount) internal override {
    uint256 _allowance = allowance[sender][spender];

    if (_allowance != UINT256_MAX) {
        require(amount <= _allowance, "ERC20: insufficient allowance");
        _approve(sender, spender, _allowance - amount);
    }
}
```

By adding the ```require(amount <= _allowance, "ERC20: insufficient allowance");``` statement, we ensure that an attempt to spend more than the allowed amount results in a transaction revert, preventing any unauthorised token transfers.

The logic, however, has some oversights:

            );

}
```

Malicious users may attempt to do native transfers with amounts set on the payload without sending any msg.value in order to spend the available InterchainTokenService native funds.
Legitimate users that want to help the protocol work by doing express executions may set amounts lower than the msg.value and not receive any sort of refund.

Manual review

function deployRemoteInterchainToken(

        bytes32 salt,
        address minter,
        string memory destinationChain,

function deployTokenManager(
        bytes32 salt,
        string calldata destinationChain,
        TokenManagerType tokenManagerType,
        bytes calldata params,
        uint256 gasValue
    ) external payable whenNotPaused returns (bytes32 tokenId) {

Manual review

Make sure to sanity check if the gasValue uint256 variable is equal to the msg.value, otherwise revert. This option would be optimal if maintaining the function's interface is crucial.

# Vulnerability details

## Summary

The deploy function in the Deployer contract attempts to transfer native tokens to the contract address before the contract is actually deployed, leading to potential loss of funds and deployment failures.

## Description

In the the `Deployer::deploy`, it tries to transfer native tokens (ETH) to the contract address that is about to be deployed. However, this transfer occurs before the actual deployment takes place which means the transfer would fail leading to potential loss of funds

The problematic code is:

```solidity
    if (msg.value > 0) {
    // slither-disable-next-line unused-return
    deployedAddress_.safeNativeTransfer(msg.value);
    }

    deployedAddress_ = _deploy(bytecode, deploySalt);
```


This sequence of operations is incorrect because it tries to send funds to an address that doesn't yet contain a contract. As a result, the transfer will fail, potentially causing the entire deployment transaction to revert or, worse, sending funds to an address that could later be controlled by an attacker.

**Illustration**

1. A user calls `deploy` function with some ETH value. 
2. The function calculates the future contract address. 
3. It attempts to transfer ETH to this address, which fails as no contract exists there yet. 
4. The actual deployment of the contract address occurs after this failed transfer.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-amplifier/interchain-token-service/src/contract.rs#L106


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `match_gateway` function has a logic bug:

```rust
fn match_gateway(storage: &dyn Storage, _: &ExecuteMsg) -> Result<Addr, Report<Error>> {
    Ok(state::load_config(storage)
        .change_context(Error::ConfigMissing)?
        .gateway)
}
```

The bug is that this function doesn't actually perform any matching or checking. It simply loads the gateway address from the config and returns it, regardless of the `ExecuteMsg` passed in.

This means that all messages will be considered as coming from the gateway, even if they aren't. The function should be comparing the sender's address (which isn't even passed to this function) with the gateway address from the config.

Additionally, the `ExecuteMsg` parameter is unused (denoted by `_`), so the function isn't considering the type of message at all, which it probably should be doing to enforce proper permissions.

## Proof of Concept


The `match_gateway` function is used in the `execute` function of the Interchain Token Service (ITS) contract to ensure permissions. However, it always returns the gateway address from config without actually checking the sender. This means any account could call the `Execute` message, which should only be callable by the gateway.

Impact:
1. An attacker could directly call `Execute` on the ITS contract, bypassing the gateway's verification.
2. This allows unauthorized cross-chain token transfers or deployments.
3. The attacker could manipulate token balances across chains, potentially minting unlimited tokens.

PoC flow:
1. Attacker calls ITS contract's `Execute` with crafted payload.
2. `match_gateway` incorrectly authorizes the call.
3. ITS processes the message, potentially transferring or minting tokens.
4. Cross-chain balance invariants are broken, compromising the entire ITS system.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-amplifier/contracts/axelarnet-gateway/src/contract/execute.rs#L77


# Vulnerability details

## Impact


The logic bug in the `route_incoming_messages` function is in the message verification process. The function checks if each incoming message exists in storage and matches the stored message, but it does not actually verify that the message has been approved or is ready for routing.

Specifically:
1. It only checks if the message exists and matches, but not its status.
2. There's no check to ensure the message has been properly verified before routing.
3. It allows routing of messages that may still be pending verification.

To fix this, the function should:
1. Check the status of each message (e.g., verified, pending, rejected).
2. Only allow routing of messages that have been fully verified and approved.
3. Reject or postpone routing for messages that are still pending or have been rejected.

This oversight could potentially allow unverified or unapproved messages to be routed, compromising the security and integrity of the cross-chain communication system.

## Proof of Concept


1. The function doesn't verify the message status before routing.
2. Messages are saved in `incoming_msg` storage upon `call_contract`, without verification.
3. `route_incoming_messages` can be called by anyone, not just the router.

Impact and PoC:
1. Attacker calls `call_contract` with malicious payload, which saves the message.
2. Attacker immediately calls `route_incoming_messages` with the same message.
3. The function finds the message in storage and routes it without verification.
4. This bypasses the entire verification process (Voting Verifier, etc.).
5. Malicious message gets routed to the destination chain via the router.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/69c4f2c3fcefb1b8eb2129af9c3685a44ae5b6fe/axelar-amplifier/contracts/axelarnet-gateway/src/contract/execute.rs#L111-L145


# Vulnerability details

### Description
Whenever messages need to be executed, the `execute` function is invoked. Inside this function, the `update_msg_status` method is called to transition the state of `msgs` from `APPROVED` to `EXECUTED`:

```javascript
pub(crate) fn execute(
    store: &mut dyn Storage,
    api: &dyn Api,
    querier: QuerierWrapper,
    cc_id: CrossChainId,
    payload: HexBinary,
) -> Result<Response, Error> {
===>    let msg = state::update_msg_status(store, cc_id.clone())
           .change_context(Error::MessageStatusUpdateFailed(cc_id))?;
```

Following this, the function carries out some additional checks until it reaches the end, where it processes the messages by invoking the `add_message` method and subsequently, an event is emitted that displays the messages to be executed

```javascript
    // Call the destination contract
    // Apps are required to expose AxelarExecutableMsg::Execute interface
    Ok(Response::new()
===>        .add_message(executable.execute(msg.cc_id.clone(), msg.source_address.clone(), payload))
===>        .add_event(AxelarnetGatewayEvent::MessageExecuted { msg }.into()))
}
```

The `add_message` function is responsible for pushing the now `EXECUTED` messages into a list of messages to be processed:

```javascript
 /// This creates a "fire and forget" message, by using `SubMsg::new()` to wrap it,
    /// and adds it to the list of messages to process.
    pub fn add_message(mut self, msg: impl Into<CosmosMsg<T>>) -> Self {
        self.messages.push(SubMsg::new(msg));
        self
    }
```

There is a discrepancy, however, between message status and actual processing. Messages are labeled as `EXECUTED` while still pending in the processing queue. As per the [Axelar Docs](https://docs.axelar.dev/dev/general-message-passing/monitoring):  `EXECUTED: informs the executed result whether it is successful or not.` In reality, messages marked as `EXECUTED` may still be awaiting processing and are therefore not finalised. 

As for the event, it will emit a `MessageExecuted` event, even though the message might still be in the processing phase and, in some cases, could remain stuck for a while. Despite this, the event will still indicate that the message has been executed.

As per the [README](https://code4rena.com/audits/2024-08-axelar-network#top):

```
- Does the message validation function accurately validate messages and update their status?
```

We believe our finding showcases that the message validation can reflect an incorrect status. 
### Recommendation
We recommend introducing logic that accurately reflects the state of a message when it is still in processing mode.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/69c4f2c3fcefb1b8eb2129af9c3685a44ae5b6fe/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L663


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
The purpose of the `contractCallWithTokenValue` function is: `Returns the amount of token that this call is worth`. The issue is that in order for a user to get the amount, they are looking for, they need to supply the same amount. This is contradictory to the entire purpose of the function and users will be unable to get the value they are looking for.

This function is important as stated by the protocol team: `These functions are queried by the express relayer to determine the value of the ITS call. They are not the main focus of the audit but support the relayer in processing transactions.` Therefore, the express relayer will be hurdled in determining the value of an ITS contract call with token.

## Impact
Due to issues in the logic of the `contractCallWithTokenValue` function, it will be practically unusable.

## Proof of Concept
As we can see in the code, `contractCallWithTokenValue` makes a call to `_checkPayloadAgainstGatewayData`:

```solidity
function contractCallWithTokenValue(
        string calldata sourceChain,
        string calldata sourceAddress,
        bytes calldata payload,
        string calldata symbol,
        uint256 amount
    ) public view virtual onlyRemoteService(sourceChain, sourceAddress) whenNotPaused returns (address, uint256) {
        _checkPayloadAgainstGatewayData(payload, symbol, amount);
        return _contractCallValue(payload);
    }
```

This is problematic, as `_checkPayloadAgainstGatewayData` requires the caller to supply `amount` as a parameter. The `amount` that the user needs to supply is the same as the `amount` that they are querying the function for, contradictory to the purpose of the function.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The `_checkPayloadAgainstGatewayData` in `contractCallWithTokenValue` is practically not needed and can be omitted.








## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L632-L643


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
Currently, in order for tokens to be transferred from one chain to another they first need to be locked/burnt on the source chain and then unlocked/minted on the destination chain. The issue is that there are several cases where the tokens will not be able to be recovered on the destination chain, causing a loss of funds for users.

## Impact
Due to the lack of a recovery function for stuck funds, users may suffer a loss of their bridged funds.

## Proof of Concept
Here are the possible scenarios where recovering tokens on the destination chain will be impossible:

1/ If the `flowLimit` becomes less than the transferred funds, before the token bridge has been executed on the destination chain, the initiator of the token transfer will not be able to recover their funds on the destination chain. The only way for this to happen would be if the `flowLimit` is increased to a value higher than the amount of tokens. This may not occur, as it will be fully dependent on the token manager operator, which may be malicious.

2/ If a `TokenManager`, corresponding to the source `tokenId`, has not been deployed on the destination chain it will be impossible for the tokens to be transferred to the destination address, as `TokenHandler.giveToken` will fail.

3/ If a destination chain changes or entirely removes another chain's trusted address, all pending transfers coming from that chain will not be executable. This will prevent users who have transferred tokens from the updated/removed chain and are yet to claim them, from ever retrieving their funds. 
This becomes much more dangerous as with the addition of the ITS Hub, many chains will change their `InterchainAddressTracker` configurations.

4/ There may not be enough locked tokens on the destination chain to transfer to the destination address. This will prevent the user from receiving their bridged tokens until more tokens are locked on the destination chain, which may never happen.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a recovery mechanism for stuck tokens on the source chain.
